title: After the flames: what this summer taught ministers about wildfires
label: 15 September 2026 · Wildfires, response and adaptation
summary: Ministers and officials from the environment and housing departments told MPs what they learned from an unprecedented UK wildfire season: the country needs better coordination between national and local players, clearer plans for aerial firefighting and water, faster practical help for farmers and land managers, and a rethink of rules about burning, land management and planning. The hearing ended with calls for urgency before next spring.

chapters.title: What happened this summer and the main lesson
chapters.takeaway: This summer’s record wildfires have changed the baseline: government says current arrangements won’t be fit for the future and wants faster, joined-up action.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: This has been a dreadful summer: record fires, homes lost and tens of thousands of acres gone. What have you learned?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: I’ve had a big fire in my constituency, so I know how real this is. We’ve had over 1,300 wildfires and our hot summer shows the risk is increasing. The headline is: what we have now won’t be fit for fires in 10 years’ time.

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: From the fire ministry view, the big lesson is that wildfires are moving to the edges of towns. Response was heroic, but we must work across government, local councils and communities on prevention, response and recovery.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So you accept we need to look again at land management, behaviour, and response—basically a step up in ambition?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: Yes. We’re scaling up in DEFRA now, building an action plan and preparing for next spring rather than waiting for a single new strategy document.

chapters.title: National coordination and the wildfire summit
chapters.takeaway: Ministers agree wildfires are a UK-wide problem and plan a summit to pull together ministers, local reps and frontline people — but they haven’t finished invitations or fixed all timelines.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Is this a national issue needing UK-wide coordination?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: Fires don’t respect borders. We need to work with devolved governments, share resources and learn from elsewhere. The Prime Minister’s wildfire summit in October should bring this together.

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: Officials are speaking regularly with Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. At official level cooperation is happening, though ministers haven’t yet all met face-to-face.

turns.speaker: Henry Tufnell
turns.text: Are devolved governments rebuffing you? Some felt the summit plans were disjointed.

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: No rebuffs. We’ve been in Scotland for a week talking to their fire service. But a ministerial lead would speed political coordination.

turns.speaker: Josh Newbury
turns.text: How will you make sure the summit includes local people like land managers and gamekeepers who actually fight fires on the ground?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: That’s crucial. The summit must be about action and include local voices. I’ll make sure we don’t just have the professionals and policy people.

chapters.title: Aerial firefighting, drones and the military
chapters.takeaway: Ministers admit the UK lacks a reliable national fleet of firefighting aircraft and are exploring national contracts, drones and military or private help before next season.

turns.speaker: Sarah Bool
turns.text: We don’t keep firefighting planes as a national fleet. Is relying on local buying of commercial planes enough?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: Aerials are high on the summit agenda. Chiefs say planes help on flames but don’t always stop ground fires. We’re looking at sea water use too—there are trade-offs with the environment.

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: Fire services worked with commercial aerial providers this summer but 44 services competing for the same asset isn’t practical. We want a cost-effective, on-call national arrangement for next summer and we’re already talking to providers.

turns.speaker: Sarah Bool
turns.text: What about drones and heavy-lift drones?

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: Drones are already used for surveillance and there’s growing water-carrying tech. They’ll be part of longer-term solutions alongside helicopters and planes.

turns.speaker: Sarah Bool
turns.text: Could we use military helicopters like Chinooks?

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: The Ministry of Defence and RAF assets are in scope. Nothing’s off the table; we’re talking with military and private sectors, but operational guarantees are complex.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You say you want things ready by next summer—do you have deadlines?

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: We aim to be in a much better place by next wildfire season and aren’t waiting for the summit. But the exact procurement and deployment mechanisms still need to be finalised.

chapters.title: Land management, controlled burning and licensing debate
chapters.takeaway: Ministers are split with land managers: DEFRA wants peatland re-wetting and stricter rules on controlled burning, while many farmers and gamekeepers say the current licensing process is too restrictive and slow.

turns.speaker: Josh Newbury
turns.text: Other countries use landscape-scale management and seasonal controlled burns. Will the UK do more prevention through land management?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: We’ll learn from abroad but adapt to UK landscapes. Peatland restoration is a big priority because wetter moors burn less and give other benefits like carbon storage and water management.

turns.speaker: Josh Newbury
turns.text: But critics say removing grazing and rewilding increased fuel on the hills. Is DEFRA rethinking that?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: Different landscapes need different management. Cutting and grazing can reduce fuel load in some places; peat restoration helps in others. Not every fire is caused by land-restoration.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The 2025 rules tightened where burning needs a licence. You’ve only issued two licences in a year—why so few?

turns.speaker: Gabrielle Edwards
turns.text: We expanded the area requiring licences (peat deeper than 30cm). We’ve seen only 24 licence applications; most were for training and the fire service advised training shouldn’t happen on deep peat because it's risky.

turns.speaker: Henry Tufnell
turns.text: Land managers tell us the licensing is complex, slow, and impractical. Natural England’s evidence used to set the rules didn’t focus on wildfire risk. Isn’t that a problem?

turns.speaker: Gabrielle Edwards
turns.text: When we set the rules we consulted widely and considered wildfire risk, biodiversity and hydrology. We take fire service advice on each licence and will keep refining guidance if it helps more sensible applications come forward.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: People on the ground say they won’t even apply under the current rules. Will you make the process more flexible before next season?

turns.speaker: Gabrielle Edwards
turns.text: We’re talking with the Country Land and Business Association and others this week to see if guidance or forms can be more practical ahead of the next season.

turns.speaker: Mr Toby Perkins
turns.text: Will the views of gamekeepers, farmers and volunteers be heard at the summit? They’re the ones risking their health to fight fires.

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: Yes. I’ll make sure local front-line voices are included. They must influence the practical outcomes.

chapters.title: Alerts, water supply and support for farmers
chapters.takeaway: The emergency phone alert was judged useful but had technical and timing problems; water shortages hampered firefighting in places and ministers are looking at faster on-farm support and permissions for ponds and reservoirs.

turns.speaker: Terry Jermy
turns.text: The emergency phone alert went to many people late—should it have been used earlier?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: The fire service advised using it and Cobra—the emergency ministers’ committee—approved it. It raised public awareness, but we’ll learn on timing and language sequencing, especially in bilingual areas like Wales.

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: The Cabinet Office actually issues the alert tech-wise. Normally Cobra or a local resilience forum requests it. We’ll write more detail to the Committee if needed.

turns.speaker: Sarah Dyke
turns.text: Water was a problem in the New Forest and elsewhere. Should water companies be forced to keep firefighting pressure during droughts?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: Water resilience is vital. We ran drought working group calls this summer with water companies and farmers. Water firms have legal duties on emergency preparedness, but we’ll review whether more specific measures are needed for firefighting.

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: Fire services have other options: high-volume pumps, drawing from lakes or the sea, and tactics needing less water. But better local water planning with companies is essential.

turns.speaker: Sarah Dyke
turns.text: Farmers want fast permission to build ponds or reservoirs and faster abstraction licences. Will you speed that up?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: We’ve put £15m toward on-farm reservoirs and are looking at planning and abstraction barriers. We’re also exploring permitted development rights so farmers can act faster where it’s practical.

chapters.title: Planning, frontline wellbeing and the next steps
chapters.takeaway: Planning can help reduce fire spread around new housing; ministers committed to better cross-government working, quicker reviews of the national risk picture, and attention to firefighter wellbeing.

turns.speaker: Charlie Dewhirst
turns.text: How should planning handle development on urban edges so new homes don’t get burnt?

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: Simple, proportionate design measures help: fire breaks, green infrastructure and materials that slow fire spread give firefighters time to respond. It’s about balancing safety with development.

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: We want wildfire risk considered alongside flood and other risks in planning, and for local resilience forums to bring that expertise into place-shaping decisions.

turns.speaker: Mr Toby Perkins
turns.text: Is the Government’s national adaptation programme up to the job? The Climate Change Committee’s verdict was harsh.

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: We accept the evidence and will be bolder in the next national adaptation plan. It’s due in 2028, but we’re not waiting—there are one-, two- and ten-year actions already under way.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You have to speed up. We’ll be back in touch. Final point: look after the people on the front line—firefighters and volunteers who’ve been through hell.

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: Agreed: firefighter health and wellbeing and community recovery are top priorities as we put new systems in place.

glossary.definition: Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, the UK government department responsible for environment, farming and rural policy.
The separate national governments for Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland with powers distinct from the UK Parliament.
A government meeting called by the Prime Minister to coordinate response and policy on wildfires across UK and stakeholders.
Aircraft used in firefighting like water-bombing planes and helicopters deployed to tackle fires from the air.
A large military transport helicopter (CH‑47 Chinook) capable of heavy lifting and sometimes used in firefighting support.
The UK government department responsible for the armed forces and national defence policy.
Royal Air Force, the United Kingdom's air force branch of the military.
Work to repair and re-wet peat soils and moorland so they store carbon and are less likely to burn.
Land where the peat layer exceeds 30 centimetres; used here as the threshold for special rules or licences on burning.
A conservation approach reducing human management so natural vegetation and wildlife recover, which can increase vegetation cover.
Information or advice provided by Natural England, the UK government body for nature conservation in England.
A UK membership organisation representing farmers, landowners and rural businesses.
COBRA is the UK government committee where senior ministers and officials coordinate national responses to major emergencies.
A local multi-agency partnership (fire, police, councils, health etc.) that plans and coordinates emergency response in an area.
A UK government department that supports the Prime Minister and coordinates the operation of government, including emergencies.
Very large pumps used to move large quantities of water quickly for firefighting or flood response.
Permissions from the regulator to take water from rivers, lakes or groundwater for uses like irrigation or filling reservoirs.
Planning rules that allow specified building or land works to proceed without a full planning application.
Natural or semi-natural features like parks, trees and ponds planned into towns to provide environmental and flood benefits.
A government strategy setting actions to adapt the country to climate change risks such as heat, flooding and wildfires.
An independent UK body that advises government on climate targets and assesses progress on adaptation and emissions.
A specific roadmap of measures and timescales the government will take to adapt to climate change impacts.
Local planning and design choices about how land and communities are developed and managed.
Small reservoirs or ponds built on farms to store water for irrigation or emergency uses like firefighting.
